confirmed: Read the entire markdown conversion, including references and Appendices A–E; independently extracted relevant PDF pages and inspected Figure 6, the results page, and image-only Appendices B and E.

The source is the 34-page journal version in Design Science, volume 12, e4 (2026), DOI 10.1017/dsj.2025.10044, by Rutvik Kokate and Prasad Onkar; received 12 May 2025, revised 27 November 2025, accepted 28 November 2025 (PDF p. 1 and page count).

The study recruited 24 first-year undergraduate design students at IIT Hyderabad; the source explicitly describes random pairing and then division into conditions, without specifying random condition allocation (PDF pp. 15–16, Section 4.6.1).

Core exclusion and criterion_2 = not_met are supported: the entire reported student pool is below 50. Retain context_class = none while treatment-allocation status is unresolved; the source does not establish a nonrandom allocation mechanism either (PDF pp. 15–16, Section 4.6.1; codebook Section 3).

The paper's 'Each of the six teams' wording and the 12 ALIA-group participants are faithfully flagged in the form; the overall team count is not unambiguously reconciled by the source (PDF p. 16, Section 4.6.1; p. 18, Section 5.2).

The output evaluation used 36 shortlisted ideas, split into two sets of 18; each set included nine ideas per condition and was rated by three experts, with six experts overall. These are idea and rater counts, not additional participants (PDF p. 13, Section 4.4.4; p. 18, Section 5.1).

Novelty and quality are scored on participants' ideas with 5-point expert ratings; quality asks about feasibility, practicality and usefulness. The with_ai questions and novelty/usefulness constructs are supported (PDF p. 13, Section 4.4.4; p. 16, Section 4.6.2).

ALIA used Mistral 7b and supplied contextual prompts during ideation; the reported session duration is 30 minutes, with stage durations 6, 8, 6 and 8 minutes (PDF pp. 11–12, Section 4.4.2; p. 25, Section 6.4.1).
Novelty reliability coefficients are alpha = 0.632 for set 1 and alpha = 0.715 for set 2 (PDF p. 18, Section 5.1).

Every number in the novelty reported string matches the cited text: ALIA M = 3.31, SD = 1.02, median = 3.00, 95% CI [3.04, 3.59]; control M = 2.21, SD = 1.11, median = 2.00, 95% CI [2.01, 2.62]; U = 770.0, p < 0.05 (PDF p. 18, Section 5.1).

The form correctly flags the control-novelty discrepancy: Figure 6 prints 2.31, whereas the results text prints 2.21. Neither value should silently replace the other (PDF p. 17, Figure 6, visually inspected; p. 18, Section 5.1).

Every number in the quality reported string matches the PDF: ALIA M = 3.22, SD = 1.25, median = 3.00; control M = 3.17, SD = 1.48, median = 3.00; U = 1431.0, p > 0.05 (PDF p. 18, Section 5.1; Figure 6 on p. 17 corroborates means and medians).

The one-line finding reproduces the means, U statistics and p-value inequalities in Section 5.1 accurately and correctly describes higher novelty with no clear quality difference; its control novelty mean is the text value, subject to the already flagged figure discrepancy (PDF pp. 17–18, Figure 6 and Section 5.1).

ACT is model_only, comparing GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Haiku and Mixtral-8x7B analogies under direct, personal and fantasy prompts; 18 analogies, six per model, were selected for expert evaluation. Its human evaluators are not human ideators assigned to AI assistance (PDF pp. 14–15, Sections 4.5.1–4.6).

This is an original human ideation experiment plus a model benchmark, not a review or meta-analysis; leaving synthesis counts and pooled estimates unset is appropriate (PDF pp. 13–16, Sections 4.4.4–4.6).
summary: The reported 24-student study falls below 50, and random assignment to the AI condition is not established. The outcome statistics match the PDF text, but design and comparator coding, analyzed counts, appendix coverage, and unresolved rater discrepancies need correction.
